title: The Fort in Coventry
originNote: Imagined from the real Labor Day weekend in Coventry, CT (Aug 29–31, 2025). The fort is invented; every place it opens onto is real.

vocab.kidDefinition: the creek near the big house — a funny, bumpy name that is fun to shout
a small tucked-away spot, just big enough to hide in
shiny metal, like a mirror on a truck
a little box that voices come out of, like a walkie-talkie
the hard grey ground outside a big building

pages.text:
The big house had so many doors.

Averill counted them.

"One, two, three... twelve," he said.

Twelve doors. And they weren't home.

Behind one door, a tiny nook.

Just their size.

Just for them.

Averill and Azi dragged in a blanket.

And a chair.

And two big cushions.

They pulled the blanket over the top.

FORT.

Dark inside. Warm. A little dusty.

A slot of daylight came through the top.

Averill's little police car crackled.

It had a radio, Averill knew.

"A giant sleeps on this farm," said the radio.

"Somewhere. Find him."

Averill and Azi looked at each other.

Azi went first, like always.

Averill went second, like always.

Out the fort's other side —

into a creek.

The reeds were taller than Azi.

The rocks were bigger than shoes.

"SKUNGAMAUG!" they shouted.

The water shushed them.

No giant here.

Back through the fort.

Out the other side.

This time —

— a horse field.

The horses had noses like doors.

Their teeth were long as a hand.

Their hooves thudded in the boys' ribs.

The horses did not mind at all.

But no giant here.

Back in the fort, the police car crackled.

"One more door," said the radio.

"Try."

Out the fort — and this time,

Averill went first.

Concrete under his feet.

One door standing wide, wide open.

Bigger than any door in the big house.

And inside —

something ENORMOUS.

Red as a fire.

Chrome as a mirror.

Fast asleep.

Bigger than a monster truck.

Bigger than a whale.

Bigger than anything.

"Found it," Averill whispered.

"Should we wake it?"

"No," said Azi. "Not today."

Back through the fort.

Back through the small door.

Back into the too-big house.

That night, Averill's police car sat on his pillow.

Somewhere on the farm, the giant slept on.

And they knew where.

story_core.notes: Portal-adventure with a real mission (find the giant), escalation across three real weekend locations reimagined as mythic, and a character reversal at the climax (Averill goes first on the mission page because it is HIS mission — payoff for the near-peer 'Azi first, Averill second' pattern set on page 6). Ends on restraint ('should we wake it?' 'not today'), which is a small maturity beat and leaves the world intact for return-play. Doctrine warns against defaulting to adventure; the buyer explicitly asked for one after the previous healing-pattern draft fell flat. Framed as celebration/witnessing per the doctrine's 'when in doubt' section — the sticky moment here is being 3.5 (soon 4.5) and away from home in a house too big for you, and the tool is a way to walk into big new places by sending your lovey first.

age_fit.notes: Rewritten for the 4–6 band. 14 pages (top of the 10–14 spec), ~317 words (mid-band), sentences mostly 3–8 words. Engagement devices for the age: a shouted funny-word (SKUNGAMAUG), a three-beat crescendo (Bigger than a monster truck. Bigger than a whale. Bigger than anything.), a call-back structure (out through the fort / back through the fort) that a 4-year-old can predict-and-shout, and a one-word page-turn beat (FORT.). Vocabulary reaches slightly (enormous, chrome, concrete) — those are also the word-tap words in the vocab list.

personalization.notes: Every real weekend detail is reincorporated as a plot beat rather than a page of scenery. Twelve doors = the actual 7BR/11-bed Airbnb ('so many doors' from the previous draft, now the counting hook that opens the book). The die-cast police car is the mission-giving radio, not a talisman. Skungamaug earns its shout and moves the plot ('no giant here'). Horses have noses like doors (echoes the door motif). The fire station is the climax the last draft wanted but never earned — approached from a mission the child was given, not stumbled into. Real relationship detail (Azi first, Averill second) is stated on page 6 and then reversed on page 11 by Averill's mission — the near-peer dynamic becomes character work instead of decoration.

craft.notes: Sensory throughout: dark, warm, dusty (fort); reeds taller than Azi, rocks bigger than shoes, water shushed (creek); noses like doors, teeth long as a hand, hooves thudding in ribs (horses); concrete under his feet, red as a fire, chrome as a mirror (fire station). No compliment loops. No teaching voice. No fabricated adults — only Averill, Azi, and a talking police car (object, per doctrine §3.1). Ends soft and bedtime-safe. Read aloud four times to check trip points; only trip is 'crackled' as a repeated verb, kept intentionally because it is the radio's sound signature.

family_tool.notes: parent-guide.md names 'The Fort Radio' — the practice of building a small enclosed space and letting the child's lovey 'report back' from wherever you are about to go. Three phrases, in-the-moment / preventive / after-the-storm scripts, and a §7 real-world rungs section for the specific new-place moments a 4-year-old is about to encounter (birthday parties, doctor visits, new classrooms, first sleepovers). Rerun ritual: 'what did the fort radio find today?' at bedtime.

rubric.pattern_used: adaptation — celebration / witnessing per authoring-doctrine.md 'When in doubt' §celebration; adventure spine at the buyer's explicit request after the previous healing-pattern draft (§7 fear-of-a-specific-thing, adapted to awe) fell flat
rubric.notes: This is the second draft for the Matthias order. The first draft (one-step-then-me) was on §7 fear-of-a-specific-thing, adapted to awe, and the family read it as a travelogue with a refrain glued on — accurate: the pattern had been softened until Averill never actually needed the tool. This draft goes celebration/witnessing per the doctrine's last section, with an adventure spine. The named tool ('The Fort Radio') is genuine (borrowable by any family with a lovey and a new-place-anxiety moment), the mission is real (find the sleeping giant), and every real weekend detail is a plot beat rather than a page of scenery. DEVIATION: doctrine step 3 says 'do not default to an adventure' — deviating explicitly because the buyer asked, and because celebration books are permitted to shift pattern per doctrine's last section (buyer wins). Rubric total 92 is honest — not 95+, because the healing-pattern rigor of §1–§10 is not fully replicated in a celebration/witnessing book; a parent whose kid is in a specific sticky moment will get less from this than from a §-matched book, and the parent guide's tool is a preventive/threshold tool rather than an in-crisis tool. That's OK: this book is about a weekend that already happened, and the tool is for the next new place.
